issues.legal_issue: A law providing for state acquisition or requisition of property is not subject to challenge under the general property-right guarantee on the ground that it imposes unreasonable restrictions.
material_facts: A statute authorized the state to requisition and acquire land, and an order was made under it requisitioning land.
The challenge to the statute argued that it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property.

The challenge relied on the contention that an earlier ruling concerning deprivation of property had displaced the precedent that excluded acquisition and requisition laws from the property-right guarantee.
issues.conclusion: The statute’s validity could not be challenged on the ground that it offended Article 19(1)(f), and it did not have to satisfy the reasonableness test in Article 19(5). The earlier ruling concerning deprivation by means other than state acquisition or requisition did not displace the rule for acquisition or requisition laws.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, state acquisition and requisition are distinct from deprivation of property in other ways under Article 31(1). A law providing for acquisition or requisition by the state is not tested under Article 19(1)(f) or Article 19(5). Kavalappara Kochuni v. State of Madras, which concerned deprivation by other means, did not decide otherwise or conflict with Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay; the earlier decisions in State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji and Lilavati Bai v. State of Bombay remained applicable to acquisition and requisition laws.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party brings a proceeding challenging the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.law_authorizes_state_acquisition_or_requ: The challenged law authorizes the state to acquire or requisition property.
predicates.challenge_uses_property_right_reasonable: The party argues that the law unreasonably restricts the right to hold property.

issues.definition: When a constitutional-validity challenge argues that a law authorizing state acquisition or requisition unreasonably restricts the right to hold property, the law is not subject to that property-right reasonableness test.
